query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, Y2O3‐doped HfB2 surface modification on boride‐based components will promote the in situ formation during molten‐aluminum exposure of a dense, adherent HfO2/Y-stabilized oxide scale that significantly retards aluminum penetration and corrosion compared to undoped HfB2 coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based component fabricated primarily from HfB2 (or similar high-melting boride) with its typical microstructural porosity and oxide inclusions from standard sintering processes.
generation.intervention: Apply an ultra-thin surface layer incorporating a low weight fraction (e.g., a few vol%) of Y2O3 into the HfB2 coating using a precision technique such as laser cladding or chemical vapor deposition.
generation.conditions: The modified component is exposed to molten aluminum conditions as used in hot-dip aluminum plating (approximately 660–750 °C) for periods on the order of 5 hours, under an inert or controlled atmosphere to simulate plating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ during exposure, the Y2O3 additive catalyzes and stabilizes the formation of a compact HfO2-based protective scale that incorporates Y ions at the oxide grain boundaries, reducing porosity and inhibiting spallation.
generation.mechanism: The rare-earth oxide (Y2O3) acts as a scale stabilizer by reducing oxide growth stress and improving adherence, thereby promoting a dense, continuous protective layer on the boride surface. This layer obstructs the interfacial diffusion between molten aluminum and the underlying boride and minimizes the destructive intermetallic reactions typical of untreated surfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under molten-aluminum exposure, the Y2O3-doped HfB2 coating is expected to show at least a 30% improvement in corrosion resistance (e.g., reduced weight gain and shallower aluminum penetration) compared to a conventional undoped HfB2 coating.
generation.baseline: The baseline is a standard HfB2 coating (or a boride-based component without Y2O3 doping) known from prior studies to form protective oxide scales that sometimes spall or are less dense in high-temperature oxidation tests.
generation.boundary: This intervention is anticipated to be effective specifically in hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions (in the temperature range of ~660–750 °C) and under steady-state exposure; its benefits for cyclic thermal stresses or in the presence of additional aggressive impurities have not been established.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on findings from PMC5126569 (which indicate that pure HfB2 shows superior oxidation resistance compared to average high-entropy borides) and from PMC10488483 (where co-doping with Y and Hf in HEA coatings improved high-temperature oxidation resistance). The extension to molten-aluminum environments is new, and uncertainties exist regarding the optimal Y2O3 concentration and the long-term stability (especially under cyclic conditions) of the resulting oxide scale.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of identically processed boride-based substrates: one group receives the standard HfB2 coating (baseline) and the other receives the ultra-thin Y2O3-doped HfB2 coating deposited by laser cladding. Subject both sets to identical molten aluminum exposures in a controlled furnace set at ~700 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform cross-sectional analyses, weight change measurements, and surface oxide characterization.
measurements: Corrosion depth and extent of aluminum penetration via cross-sectional SEM
Phase analysis and oxide scale continuity using XRD and EDS
Adhesion and porosity characteristics of the oxide scale via high-magnification microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y2O3-doped HfB2 coated samples do not demonstrate at least a 30% reduction in corrosion indicators (e.g., weight gain, depth of aluminum penetration) and do not exhibit noticeably denser, more adherent oxide scales compared to the undoped HfB2 samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application.
